title: How to write report card comments faster on Mac: a teacher's routine for Pages

intro: To write report card comments faster, stop starting from a blank page. Build a bank of sentences you already trust, fill in the student-specific parts last, and batch the work into fixed sessions. No study times report card comments alone, so you need your own numbers. This guide covers what the work costs, why it piles up, free fixes you can use on a Mac, and where Lazur can help.
tldr: A 2022 Education Week survey found a median 5 hours a week on grading and feedback for teachers.
No study times report card comments, so measure your own minutes for one class this term.
Build a comment bank, write each comment in three parts, and fill in names last.
Pages mail merge can fill repeated parts. Test it on one student before the whole class.
AI drafts are not a proven time saver yet. Check your school's data rules first.

blocks.text: How long report card comments take

Nobody times report card comments on their own. The closest data comes from a 2022 Education Week survey. It found a median 54 hours of total work each week for teachers. Of that, a median 3 hours went to general administrative work, and 5 hours went to grading and providing feedback on student work. Comments fall inside that feedback time, but the survey does not split them out.

That gap matters for planning. You might lose one evening to comments or a whole weekend, and no source tells you which. Measure your own time instead. The tracking section below shows how, and the figures above give the context.
Why comments pile up at the end of the term

Most comments get written in one rush. The term ends, the portal opens, and the deadline lands on a week that already holds grading and planning. Speed drops when all the work is due at once. Quality drops with it, because tired writing tends to be shorter and vaguer.

items: You start from a blank page for every student, even when most sentences repeat.
The evidence lives in too many places: the gradebook, paper notes and memory.
Comments arrive after grading, so you have little energy left to write them.
No shared standard sets the tone, so each comment gets rebuilt from zero.

blocks.text: None of this is a personal failing. The schedule creates the rush. The fix is to move small pieces of the work earlier, into weekly habits, and to keep the repeated parts in one place.
A worked example: one comment in three parts

Say you teach science and want to comment on a student named Maya. Her notes show that she improved her lab write-ups and struggled with data tables in the spring. Built from scratch, that comment could take a long time to phrase. Built from parts, it goes faster. This is an example, not a real student.
Start with a strength you can prove. Add one piece of evidence from the term. Finish with one next step she can act on. The table shows each part filled in.

rows: Names one thing the student did well
Maya wrote clearer conclusions in her lab reports this term.
Points to a specific moment or piece of work
Her data tables were accurate by the spring unit.
Gives one action the student can take
Next, she can practice labelling axes before each table.
blocks.caption: A three-part comment. Each part can come from your bank or your notes.

blocks.text: The structure matters more than the wording. Once you see the three parts, you fill them in order. You stop hunting for the perfect opening line, and most comments come out faster and more specific.
Keep a comment bank you can reuse

A comment bank is only useful if it sounds like you. Write it during a quiet week, not during report card week. Add a sentence each time a comment works well. Delete any line that reads like a template to a parent. Review the whole bank once per term, since your class changes.
Fill placeholders and check every name

Placeholders fail in predictable ways. A name you replace in one spot can stay wrong in another. A placeholder you forget to fill can slip into a final report. After you finish, search for each student's name and check that it appears only where you expect it.
Use mail merge in Pages for repeated parts

Apple's Pages guide says you can use mail merge to automatically personalize multiple documents. You point it at a source file, and each row fills one document. For report cards, the source might be a spreadsheet with one row per student. Pages 15.4 requires macOS 26 or later, so check your version first.

Apple does not present mail merge as a report card feature. No source measures its time savings either. Test it on one student before you run the whole class. Compare the output with your gradebook and read every line. A blank field can produce a sentence that reads badly.
Where AI tools help and where they do not yet

The evidence on AI and teacher time is thin. A randomized trial in Turkey assigned 193 teachers to a ChatGPT-based teaching assistant or to teach as usual for 10 weeks in spring 2025. Average achievement did not change overall. Students with the tool rated their classes with a modest decline in enjoyment, interest and importance. The study is a draft that has not been peer-reviewed, and it covered feedback and lesson materials, not report cards.

The lead author's view on AI for their own materials is blunt: 'It's not a time saver.' The article gives no measured figure for hours saved. Treat big time-saving claims with care, including your own early impressions.

Microsoft's Teach feature covers lesson plans, rubrics, quizzes and flashcards. Its support page does not list an in-app comment or report card tool. Apple's Writing Tools suit the final pass better than the first draft, since they proofread and rewrite text you already wrote.

Try any helper on comments you have already written. Compare its output with your own version for a student you know well. If the tool's version misses the evidence, keep your bank and skip the tool. Read the full terms of any service before you paste school material into it.

blocks.title: Student data comes first
blocks.text: Do not paste student names, grades or records into any tool unless your school allows it. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and screenshots still go to AI providers to answer, so your school's rules still apply.
Common mistakes that make comments slower

items: Polishing the first comment, then expecting every later comment to match it.
Waiting until grading ends to think about each student's evidence.
Using one closing line for the whole class, so parents spot the template.
Skipping the name check, then fixing an error after the report goes home.
Pasting student details into a tool before you know what your school allows.

blocks.text: The first mistake costs the most time. A good comment needs one true, specific idea in each part. A plain sentence that says something real beats a polished one that says nothing. Accept the plain sentence and move on.
Students who need extra care

Some students need comments that take more care. A student with an education plan may need wording that matches that plan. A student who had a hard term may need an honest comment that stays kind. Draft these by hand first, then check them against your school's guidance.

Regulated information needs the most care. If your school or employer has rules about student records, follow them. Do not paste private details into an AI tool unless your employer allows it. Ask your administrator when the rule is unclear.
How to tell if the system is working

Measure before you change anything. Note how long the first class takes this term, from opening the file to saving it. Repeat the note for the next class. A simple log beats a guess. If the time drops, keep the habit. If it does not, find the step that still takes longest.

Watch quality too. Read the comments a week after you save them. Do they still sound like the student? If they sound like every other comment in the bank, the bank needs more specific lines, not more polish.
Where to start on a school night

Start with one class and one part of the process. Build the bank for strengths only. Keep the weekly note for that class. Once that feels normal, add the mail merge test. Small steps keep the work from taking over your evenings.
Pages users can read the [Pages guide for teachers](/for/teachers/pages) for templates and mail merge notes. Parent replies are covered in the [Gmail guide for teachers](/for/teachers/gmail).

Lazur can help with the parts that need a voice or a second pair of eyes. It answers questions out loud, points at controls and types text you dictate. Lazur drafts text when you ask, but you decide what goes home.

faq.question: Can AI help me write report card comments faster?
faq.answer: Maybe, but the evidence is thin. A non-peer-reviewed Turkey trial found no overall change in student achievement. Its lead author said AI is 'not a time saver' for their own materials. Test any tool on comments you have already written, and check your school's data rules before you paste anything.

faq.question: Does Pages have a report card template?
faq.answer: Apple does not describe a report card template in its Pages guide. Pages does offer mail merge, which Apple says can personalize multiple documents from source files. Search Pages Help for mail merge and follow the steps for your version. Pages 15.4 requires macOS 26 or later.

faq.question: Is Pages free to use?
faq.answer: Apple says Pages remains free. Customers keep free access to the existing Keynote, Pages, Numbers and Freeform apps and features. Apple Creator Studio is a separate subscription at $12.99 per month in the US, or $2.99 per month for verified college students and educators. Confirm current prices on Apple's Creator Studio page.

faq.question: Does Microsoft Teach write report card comments?
faq.answer: Not as far as its support page shows. Microsoft lists Lesson Plan, Rubric, Quiz and Flashcards, and no comment or report card tool. Teach is for eligible faculty and staff with a Microsoft 365 for Education license. It is not available to students or consumer accounts.

faq.question: Does Lazur write my report card comments?
faq.answer: Lazur drafts and types text when you ask. Hold fn to dictate your own sentence at the cursor, or ask Lazur to draft from your notes. You read and edit every line before it goes home. Lazur does not click buttons or operate Pages for you.

faq.question: What does Lazur do with student information?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Your school's rules still decide what you may share, so check them first.

faq.question: How do I measure whether faster comments are actually faster?
faq.answer: No study times report card comments, so you need your own log. Write down the minutes for one class this term, from opening the file to saving it. Repeat the log next term with the same method, then compare the totals before you decide a method works.

faq.question: Why do my comments still sound generic with a bank?
faq.answer: A bank without evidence produces vague praise. Add one specific, dated fact to each comment, such as a named project or a skill from the term. Replace any line that would fit every child in the class.

costs.title: Evenings and weekends
costs.text: A 2022 Education Week survey found a median 54 hours of total work per week for teachers. About 5 hours of that went to grading and providing feedback. Report card comments sit inside that feedback time, but the survey does not measure them alone. Every comment written from scratch adds to a week that already runs long.

costs.title: Comments that sound generic
costs.text: Comments written at speed drift toward lines like 'Great effort' and 'Keep it up.' Parents read them and notice. A comment that could fit any child tells a family very little. The cost is not only your time. It is the trust a comment is supposed to build.

costs.title: A heavier load for teachers
costs.text: Burnout is up. A RAND figure reported by K-12 Dive puts teacher burnout at 57% in 2026, up from 54% in 2021. The article cites RAND without naming the report, so treat the number as secondhand. Report card season adds weight to a load that is already heavy.

costs.title: Late-evening mistakes
costs.text: A comment written late in the evening carries more errors. A wrong name, a wrong subject or a sentence meant for another student can slip through. Each error costs a correction later, and sometimes a hard conversation with a family. Fast writing needs a check at the end.

costs.title: Subscriptions add up
costs.text: Some helpers cost money. Apple Creator Studio costs $12.99 per month, or $129 per year, in the US after the free trial. Verified educators pay $2.99 per month. MagicSchool's Plus plan lists $12.99 per month billed monthly. Pages itself stays free, and you do not need a subscription for the methods here.

causes.title: The comment starts from a blank page
causes.text: Writing from nothing takes longer than editing. Each student needs a new opening, a new strength and a new next step. Most teachers repeat the same ideas for every child. The ideas repeat, so the wording can be reused instead of invented each time.

causes.title: Evidence is scattered across tools
causes.text: The proof for a comment lives in many places. A quiz score sits in the gradebook, a lab note sits on paper, and a good class discussion lives in your memory. When you sit down to write, you rebuild that picture from scratch. Recall takes time, so it often gets skipped and replaced with a vague line.

causes.title: Feedback is the last job of the week
causes.text: Grading and feedback take a median 5 hours a week, according to the 2022 Education Week survey. Report card comments arrive on top of that work. They often come all at once at the end of the term. Tired writing tends to be shorter and vaguer than rested writing.

causes.title: Nothing sets a shared standard
causes.text: Each comment feels like a standalone piece of writing. You check tone, length and accuracy from zero every time. Without a standard, you decide the rules again for every child. A shared structure cuts those decisions down to a few quick questions per student.

causes.title: Your tools skip the repeated part
causes.text: Mail merge in Pages fills repeated parts from a source file. Apple does not describe it as a report card feature. Microsoft's Teach feature covers lesson plans, rubrics, quizzes and flashcards, and its support page lists no comment tool. You will likely build the system yourself.

causes.title: Nobody measures the time
causes.text: No study times report card comments, and no trial tests a fix for them. That makes the cost easy to miss. Without numbers, a slow process looks normal. Your own log is the only reliable way to see where the minutes go.

fixes.title: Build one comment bank
fixes.text: Make one document called Comment bank in Pages or Google Docs. Sort sentences under four headings: strengths, growth, next steps and closing lines. Write a few options under each heading. Keep the bank open beside your gradebook, so you can copy from it without switching windows.

fixes.title: Use placeholders for names
fixes.text: Write [Name] and [skill] in the bank wherever a student's details go. In Pages, press ⌘F to search for each placeholder. In Google Docs, press ⌘⇧H to open Find and replace. Replace each placeholder with the real value, then search for the student's name to confirm it appears where you expect.

fixes.title: Write each comment in three parts
fixes.text: Start with one strength you can prove. Add one piece of evidence from this term, such as a project, a quiz topic or a class moment. End with one next step the student can act on. Three short parts keep each comment specific and keep the writing short.

fixes.title: Keep a weekly note per student
fixes.text: Open Apple Notes and make one note per class. After each lesson where you saw real work, add one dated line per student. A line such as 'Led the group discussion on Tuesday' takes seconds. By the end of the term, you have a record to pull from instead of memory.

fixes.title: Batch the writing into sessions
fixes.text: Write all the strength sentences in one sitting, then all the evidence lines in another. Ask Siri to set a timer for each session, and stop when it rings. Batching keeps your attention on one type of sentence. Switching tasks with every comment slows you down.

fixes.title: Test mail merge on one student
fixes.text: Apple's Pages guide says mail merge can automatically personalize multiple documents from source files. Build a template with placeholders for name, class and subject. Merge one student first, then compare the result with your gradebook before you run the whole class. Search Pages Help for mail merge, since menus can change between releases.

fixes.title: Tighten your sentences, do not generate them
fixes.text: If your Mac supports Apple's Writing Tools, you can proofread or rewrite text you already wrote. Apple's guide lists Proofread, Rewrite with tones such as Friendly, Professional or Concise, and Summarize. The guide covers macOS 27, and availability varies by region and language. Use it on your own sentences, then read the result aloud before you keep it.

fixes.title: Check names and facts last
fixes.text: Read every comment once more before you save. Check the name, subject, grade and any fact about the student's work. Compare each name with the gradebook. A short final pass catches the errors that late writing creates.

fixes.title: Check your school's rule before you paste
fixes.text: Find your school's rule on student data before you paste anything into an AI tool. If the rule is unclear, ask your administrator. Keep names and private details out of prompts unless the rule allows them. Follow your employer's rules first, even when a tool's settings look safe.

plan.label: Monday
plan.title: Pick the four headings
plan.text: Choose one class. List the four headings for the comment bank: strengths, growth, next steps and closing lines. Write two options under each heading. Keep the file open for the rest of the week.

plan.label: Tuesday
plan.title: Start the notes habit
plan.text: Open Apple Notes and make one note per class. After each lesson where you saw real work, add one dated line per student. Keep lines short, so the habit survives a busy day.

plan.label: Wednesday
plan.title: Test mail merge
plan.text: Make a Pages template with placeholders for name, class and subject. Run the merge for one student. Compare the output with your gradebook before you use it for the class.

plan.label: Thursday
plan.title: Batch the writing
plan.text: Ask Siri to set a timer for one session. Write the strength sentences for the whole class in that sitting. Stop when the timer rings, then start the evidence lines the next day.

plan.label: Friday
plan.title: Read and check
plan.text: Read each comment aloud. Search for each name with ⌘F in Pages or ⌘⇧H in Google Docs. Confirm names, subjects and grades match your records. Save the finished file in your school's approved location.

plan.label: Weekend
plan.title: Record the time
plan.text: Write down how long the class took from start to save. Compare that total with the first log, if you have one. Decide what to change before the next class.
